inline_comments.comment: `useHtmlLabels` is being passed as the `addBackground` argument (5th parameter) to `createLabel`. These are semantically different: `addBackground` controls whether to apply the `labelBkg` CSS class (a visual background), while `useHtmlLabels` controls whether HTML rendering is used at all. When `useHtmlLabels` is `true`, this inadvertently adds a background to edge terminal labels (startLabelLeft, startLabelRight, endLabelLeft, endLabelRight), which is unintended. The same bug appears in all four terminal label calls. The 5th argument should be `false` for all of these calls.

`labelHelper` is used by many diagram types (ER, state, class, etc.), but the config path has been narrowed to `getConfig()?.flowchart?.htmlLabels`. For non-flowchart diagrams, this may not reflect the correct diagram-specific `htmlLabels` setting — for example, `classdiagram.htmlLabels` defaults to `false` while `flowchart.htmlLabels` defaults to `true`. A node in a class diagram that relied on its own `htmlLabels: false` config could now accidentally fall through to the flowchart default. Consider using the diagram-type-aware config or documenting why `flowchart` is the right fallback for all diagrams.

`applyStyle` is called with `node.labelStyle` on both the `span` (line 55) and the `div` (line 58). The `span` is the correct target for label typography — applying the same style to the `div` wrapper is redundant and can cause double-cascading for inherited properties like `font-size` or `color`. Consider removing the `applyStyle(div, node.labelStyle)` call, which was present in the old code but is now superseded by the explicit span styling.

`getWrappingWidth()` reads from `getConfig().flowchart?.wrappingWidth`, but `createLabel` is also called from non-flowchart diagrams (e.g. ER diagrams via `rectWithTitle.ts`, subgraph clusters). For those diagrams `flowchart.wrappingWidth` is not the configured value, so it silently falls back to the hardcoded `DEFAULT_WRAPPING_WIDTH = 200`. At minimum, this should be documented; ideally the caller should pass the width explicitly (as some callers do) rather than relying on this fallback.

`getConfig()` is called twice in the same ternary (lines 26–27). The function is not free — it performs a config merge/lookup. Cache the result once:
```ts
const cfg = getConfig();
const bodyFontSize = cfg.fontSize
  ? cfg.fontSize
  : window.getComputedStyle(document.body).fontSize;
```

The `new Promise` on line 19 is missing its TypeScript type parameter. Since `res(img)` resolves with an `HTMLImageElement` but the resolved value is discarded by `Promise.all`, the correct annotation is `new Promise<void>((res) => { ... res(); })` or passing the image value as `new Promise<HTMLImageElement>((res) => { ... res(img); })`. The untyped form produces an implicit `Promise<unknown>`, which weakens type safety in the surrounding `Promise.all` call.

The JSDoc block on lines 10–17 describes `configureLabelImages` (its parameters, return type, and purpose) but is placed immediately before `export const labelHelper`. IDEs and documentation generators will attach this doc block to `labelHelper`, producing incorrect API docs. Either remove the comment here (since the function is documented at its declaration in `labelImageUtils.ts`) or add a blank line and a proper `// See configureLabelImages` inline comment instead.

The changeset is marked as `patch`, but this PR enables new user-visible features — KaTeX rendering and iconpack/FontAwesome icons — in `createLabel` code paths that previously lacked them. Per the contribution guidelines referenced in the PR's own checklist: "Changesets that add features should be `minor`". Consider bumping this to `minor` and updating the message prefix from `fix:` to `feat:`.

general_comments.comment: The old `addHtmlLabel` applied `padding-right: 1px` with a comment "Fix for firefox". This line is silently removed in the refactored version with no explanation or replacement. Browser-specific workarounds of this kind tend to encode hard-won knowledge about rendering edge cases. If the Firefox issue is genuinely resolved by the new rendering approach, that should be noted in a comment; if it was simply forgotten, its absence could cause a visual regression in Firefox where labels are clipped or cause unwanted reflow.
